description: Poludnitsa (Lady Midday) is a Slavic noon-wraith who appears in fields at midday during harvest. She takes the form of a young woman in white, an old hag, or a girl, carrying a scythe or shears. She stops workers to ask difficult questions; failure to answer brings heatstroke, madness, or death. She personifies sunstroke and enforces the taboo against working at high noon.
source: Dixon-Kennedy, Encyclopedia of Russian and Slavic Myth and Legend; Ralston, Songs of the Russian People; Podgórska & Podgórski, Wielka Księga Demonów Polskich
research_notes: Well-documented across Slavic cultures (Polish Południca, Czech Polednice, Serbian Poludnica). The record's 'ghost' type should be 'demon' — she is a personification of sunstroke, not a dead spirit.

description: Poroniec is a Polish demon born from stillborn or unbaptized infants. It haunts crossroads and graveyards, causing stillbirths and infant mortality. If buried under the house threshold, it becomes a protective kłobuk house spirit instead. Related to the Scandinavian myling. Reflects Christian anxiety about unbaptized souls.
source: Podgórska & Podgórski, Wielka Księga Demonów Polskich; Szyjewski, Religia Słowian; Wikipedia (Poroniec)
research_notes: Attested in Polish folklore collections. The record correctly identifies it as a demon; the 'seduce' behavior tag is inaccurate — poroniec does not seduce.

description: Potopica is a Serbian water nymph (siren) inhabiting springs and rivers. She appears as a beautiful maiden combing her long hair. If approached respectfully she grants wishes; if rejected she lures men into the water to drown. Part of the broader South Slavic vila/rusalka complex of water maidens.
source: Serbian folklore collections; Vuk Karadžić, Srpske narodne pjesme; comparative Slavic water spirit lore
research_notes: Name derives from 'topiti' (to drown). Less documented than rusalka/vila but attested in Serbian oral tradition as a local water nymph variant.

description: Povitrulya is a Ukrainian wind spirit from the Carpathian Mountains, daughter of the mountain winds. She appears as a winged, flower-clad maiden who flies without touching ground. She helps lovers and shepherds; a man who steals her wings can marry her, but she will flee if she recovers them. A positive, benevolent spirit of the air.
source: Ukrainian Wikipedia (Повітруля); Ukrainian Small Encyclopedia (Buenos Aires 1963); Tykhovska, Etnopsychologichna specifika obrazu Povitruli
research_notes: Well-attested in Transcarpathian Ukrainian folklore. The record's 'earth' element is incorrect — she is an air/wind spirit. 'Seduce' behavior tag is misleading; she helps lovers but is not predatory.

description: Płanetnik (also chmurnik, obłocznik) is a Polish demonic cloud spirit — the soul of a suicide or sudden-death victim who controls storms and hail. Appears as a tall old man in a wide hat or a small creature. Can be benevolent (warning of storms) or malevolent. Gains favor by throwing flour into wind or fire. Fights storm-dragons in the clouds. Also a term for weather-divining shamans.
source: Strzelczyk, Mity, podania i wierzenia dawnych Słowian; Podgórska & Podgórski, Wielka Księga Demonów Polskich; Kempiński, Encyklopedia mitologii ludów indoeuropejskich; Wikipedia (Płanetnik)
research_notes: Well-documented in Polish folklore. The record's 'forest-spirit' archetype and 'earth' element are wrong — he is a sky/weather spirit. 'Protective, benevolent' tags only capture half his nature; he is explicitly demonic and ambivalent.

description: Vampir is the Serbian vampire — the etymological root of the English word 'vampire'. An animated corpse rising from the grave at night to drink blood of the living. Created by suicide, excommunication, caul birth, or animal jumping over corpse. The 18th-century cases of Petar Blagojevich and Arnold Paole sparked the European vampire controversy. Warded by garlic, crosses, holy water.
source: Calmet, Dissertation sur les vampires; Flückinger, Visum et Repertum (1732); Barber, Vampires, Burial, and Death; Wikipedia (Vampire folklore by region — Slavic Europe)
research_notes: Best-documented Slavic vampire tradition. The record is accurate; Serbian 'vampir' is the source of the German 'Vampir' and English 'vampire'.

description: Veshtitza is a Montenegrin witch-vampire whose soul leaves her body at night in the form of a black hen or moth to scout homes with children. She returns to drain blood and consume hearts. By day she appears as an ordinary woman. A South Slavic variant of the striga/shtriga, blending witch and vampire traits. Feared as a night predator of infants.
source: Montenegrin folklore collections; comparative South Slavic vampire-witch lore (striga, shtriga, mora); Wikipedia (Vampire folklore by region)
research_notes: Attested in Montenegrin/Serbian borderland folklore. The record correctly identifies the black hen/moth soul-flight motif. Distinct from the Serbian 'veshtica' (witch) by the vampire feeding behavior.

description: Vještica is the Croatian/Serbian word for 'witch' (from 'vješti' — to know), not a distinct creature. The record appears to conflate the general term with a specific ogre. Actual Croatian witch beliefs involve night flight on wooden beams, causing storms, illness, and infertility.
source: Croatian Wikipedia (Vještica — surname page only); Croatian folklore surveys (Kajkavian/Štokavian); comparative Slavic witch lore
research_notes: The creature as described (ogre named Vještica) is not independently attested. 'Vještica' is a common noun for 'witch' and a surname. The record's type 'ogre' and traits 'devouring, curses' are generic misassignments. Closest real analogue: Croatian vještica (witch) or Bosnian mora (nightmare witch).

description: Vodník is the Czech male water spirit, ruler of rivers and ponds. He appears as a green-clad man with a dripping coat, or as a frog. Uses colored ribbons to lure victims into water, storing their souls in porcelain pots in his underwater palace. Can be benevolent (helping fishermen) or malevolent (drowning bathers). His wife is frog-like. Friday is his day off from man-snatching.
source: Grohmann, Aberglauben und Bräuche aus Böhmen und Mähren; Erben, Kytice; Polívka, Národní pohádky; Dvořák, symphonic poem Vodník; Wikipedia (Vodyanoy — Czech/Slovak sections)
research_notes: Well-documented in Czech folklore and literature. Distinct from Russian vodyanoy by the ribbon-lure and soul-pot motifs. The record's 'siren' type is incorrect — he is a male water goblin.

description: Vodník is the Slovak water spirit, nearly identical to the Czech Vodník. Inhabits Orava region lakes and rivers. Uses ribbons to lure humans, stores drowned souls in pots. His wife appears as a frog; a widespread tale has a woman serve as godmother to the vodník's frog-wife and free captive souls. Can be helpful to fishermen who offer tobacco.
source: Polívka, Slovenské pohľady na vodníka; Grohmann, Böhmen und Mähren; Wikipedia (Vodyanoy — Slovakia section); Matija Valjavec, Slovenski glasnik
research_notes: Well-attested in Slovak folklore, especially Orava. The record duplicates the Czech entry; Slovak vodník has stronger frog-wife and godmother tale motifs.

description: Vodyanoy (dedushka vodyanoy) is the East Slavic male water spirit, ruler of rivers, lakes, and millponds. Appears as a naked, green-haired old man with a pot belly, covered in slime and weeds, or as a giant catfish/frog. Demands blood sacrifices (livestock, historically human) when mills are built. Helps fishermen who offer butter; drowns the disrespectful. Rides a wels catfish.
source: Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki; Machal, Slavic Mythology; Dixon-Kennedy, Encyclopedia of Russian and Slavic Myth; Wikipedia (Vodyanoy)
research_notes: One of the best-documented Slavic spirits. The record is accurate but 'water-spirit' archetype is correct while 'ghost' type for poludnitsa was wrong — vodyanoy is a place spirit, not undead.

description: Vukodlak (volkolak, vovkulaka) is the Slavic werewolf — a human shapeshifter who temporarily becomes a wolf. Most detailed beliefs among Belarusians, Poles, and Ukrainians; South Slavs conflate it with vampires. Transformation via sorcery (rolling over knives, crawling through horse collar), curse, or birth predisposition. Retains human intelligence but cannot speak.
source: Ivanov & Toporov, research on Slavic werewolf; Vlasova, Novaya abevega russkikh sueveriy; Wikipedia (Werewolf in Slavic mythology); Herodotus, Histories 4.105
research_notes: Pan-Slavic but regionally variable. The record's 'werewolf' type and 'Serbia' culture are fine; the concept appears across all Slavic peoples. 'Lycanthropic strength' and 'pack hunting' are modern gaming additions not in folklore.

description: Od Iedeh is the Evenki (Siberian Tungusic) fire spirit, mistress of the hearth. Appears as a face in the flames or an old woman made of fire, sometimes riding a fox. Must be respected with offerings; protects the household, aids cooking and warmth, but burns the dwelling if insulted. Communicates through crackling flames. Central to Evenki shamanic practice.
source: Evenki shamanic folklore collections; Varlamova & Simonov, Mify narodov Sibiri; Okladnikov, Drevnyaya istoriya narodov Sibiri; Anisimov, Religia evenkov
research_notes: Attested in Evenki oral tradition. The record's 'Russia/Siberia' culture is correct but 'forest-spirit' archetype is wrong — she is a hearth/fire spirit. 'Animal communication, possession' strengths are generic shamanic traits, not specific to her.

description: Zhar-Ptitsa (Firebird) is the Slavic magical glowing bird from a faraway land. Its golden feathers illuminate darkness; a single feather lights a room. Both a blessing and a harbinger of doom to its captor. Central to quest tales (Ivan Tsarevich and the Grey Wolf) where heroes seek it for a tsar. Inspired Stravinsky's ballet The Firebird. Parallel to Armenian Hazaran Blbul and Iranian Simurgh.
source: Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki (tale 168); Massie, Land of the Firebird; Stravinsky/Fokine/Benois, The Firebird ballet; Reymont, Chłopi (Nobel novel citing firebirds); Wikipedia (Firebird)
research_notes: Iconic Slavic folklore figure. The record is accurate. 'Curse, bless' behavior tags capture its dual nature well.

description: Zlydzens (Belarusian zlydni, Ukrainian zlydni) are small, hunchbacked, hazardous stove spirits living under the masonry oven. They wear big boots and earflap hats, resemble cat-dog hybrids. In groups they wreck utensils, spill milk, create chaos; drawn to greedy households. Cowardly alone. The Ukrainian phrase 'zhyty v zlydnyakh' (live in zlydni) means 'to live in poverty.'
source: Brouka, Magical World: From Belarusian Myths; Rybakov, Ancient Slavic Paganism; Tsybulkin et al., Vlesova kniga; Wikipedia (Zlydzens)
research_notes: Well-attested in Belarusian/Ukrainian folklore. The record's 'trickster' type fits; 'shapeshifter' archetype is incorrect — they do not shapeshift. 'Flight' strength is wrong.

description: Zmaj is the Serbian dragon — a winged serpent dwelling in caves near villages. In Balkans lore, unlike the malevolent Russian zmey, the zmaj is often a benevolent guardian who fights the evil ala/lamia (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man, fire bird, or smoke; takes human lovers (e.g., Tsarina Milica). Symbol of patriotic resistance against Ottoman rule.
source: Karadžić, Srpske narodne pjesme; Petrovitch, Hero Tales and Legends of the Serbs; MacDermott, Bulgarian Folk Songs; Wikipedia (Slavic dragon — Zmaj of Serbian fairy tales)
research_notes: Distinct from Russian zmey gorynych. The record's 'water-spirit' archetype is wrong — zmaj is a fire/sky dragon. 'Heat generation, flight' strengths are accurate; 'lack of fuel' weakness is a modern gaming addition.

description: Zmej is the Bulgarian dragon — a winged, scale-covered serpent, often with multiple heads (3–12). Unlike East Slavic malevolent zmey, the Balkan zmej is a benevolent guardian who fights the lamia/hala (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man to woo human women; children of such unions become vampire hunters. Symbol of patriotic resistance. St.
source: Georgieva, Bǎlgarska narodna mitologiya; MacDermott, Bulgarian Folk Songs; Slaveykov, folk collections; Marinov, St. George songs; Wikipedia (Slavic dragon — Balkan Slavic dragons)
research_notes: Well-documented in Bulgarian folklore. The record's 'demonic-entity' archetype is wrong for the Balkan zmej (it applies to lamia/hala). 'Fire breath, armored scales' are accurate.

description: Zmey Gorynych is the iconic Russian three-to-twelve-headed dragon of byliny and fairy tales. Dwells beyond three rivers or in mountain caves. Each severed head regenerates unless cauterized; kidnaps princesses; breathes fire. Slain by bogatyrs Dobrynya Nikitich and Ilya Muromets. A specific named antagonist, not a species. Name means 'serpent of the mountains (Goryny).'
source: Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki; Bilibin illustrations; Ralston, Russian Folk-Tales; Dobrynya Nikitich rescues Zabava (bylina); Wikipedia (Zmey Gorynych, Slavic dragon)
research_notes: Most famous Russian dragon. The record's 'water-spirit' archetype is incorrect — he is a fire/mountain dragon. 'Storm calling' strength is plausible (weather association).

description: Nav (Polish Nawia, Ukrainian Mavka/Nyavka) denotes both the souls of the prematurely dead (tragic deaths, suicides, drowned, warlocks) and the Slavic underworld ruled by Veles. As spirits (nawie), they appear as birds, hostile and jealous of the living. As a place, Nav lies across a living sea or deep underground, guarded by a zmey; souls later reincarnate.
source: Szyjewski, Religia Słowian; Strzelczyk, Mity dawnych Słowian; Kempiński, Encyklopedia mitologii; Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let); Warner, Russian Peasant Beliefs; Wikipedia (Nav)
research_notes: Fundamental Slavic eschatological concept. The record's 'demon' type and 'water-spirit' archetype are category errors — Nav is a category of souls and a cosmological realm, not a single creature.

description: Nica (or Nika) is a Bulgarian water nymph, cognate with Russian rusalka and South Slavic samodiva/vila. Inhabits rivers and lakes as a beautiful young woman with long hair. Can be helpful to fishermen but dangerous if scorned, drowning swimmers. Part of the broader Slavic 'water maiden' complex. The name may derive from 'nica' (water spirit) in Bulgarian dialect.
source: Bulgarian folklore collections; Georgieva, Bǎlgarska narodna mitologiya; comparative Slavic water spirit lore (rusalka, samodiva, vila); Wikipedia (Samodiva, Rusalka)
research_notes: Attested in Bulgarian folklore but less documented than rusalka. The record is essentially accurate; 'dangerous, helpful' behavior tags fit the ambivalent water maiden archetype.

description: Wodnik is the Polish male water spirit, ruler of lakes, rivers, ponds, and millponds. Documented by Oskar Kolberg in Pomeranian and Masovian materials. Controls aquatic creatures; drowns those who disrespect his waters. Fishermen offer tobacco for good catches. Appears as a green-clad man or naked figure. West Slavic counterpart to Czech Vodník and Russian Vodyanoy.
source: Kolberg, Lud (Pomeranian/Masovian volumes); Strzelczyk, Mity dawnych Słowian; Podgórska & Podgórski, Wielka Księga Demonów Polskich; Wikipedia (Vodyanoy — Polish Topielec section)
research_notes: Well-documented in Polish ethnography. The record is accurate. Kolberg's fieldwork gives it strong source quality.

description: Baba Yaga is the iconic East Slavic witch: a gaunt crone with iron teeth who dwells in a hut on chicken legs deep in the forest. Flies in a mortar, steers with a pestle, sweeps tracks with a broom. Tests visitors with three impossible tasks; rewards cleverness with magical gifts, devours the failures. Commands forest creatures.
source: Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki; Johns, Baba Yaga: The Ambiguous Mother and Witch of the Russian Fairy Tale; Lomonosov, Russian Grammar (1755); Propp, Historical Roots of the Wonder Tale; Wikipedia (Baba Yaga)
research_notes: One of the most famous Slavic folklore figures. The record's detailed appearance/behavior text is accurate but appears to describe the Polish variant (Masovian oak groves). Russian Baba Yaga is the primary attestation.

description: Baba Yaga (Polish Baba Jaga, Czech Ježibaba) is the West Slavic forest witch, closely related to the Russian figure. Dwells in a hut on chicken legs in dense Masovian oak forests. Same mortar/pestle/broom attributes, same three-task tests. May reflect Finno-Ugric influence (stilt-storehouse huts). Ježibaba differs in appearance and tale types.
source: Polish folklore collections; Johns, Baba Yaga (on West Slavic variants); Hubbs, Jędza; Grohmann, Ježibaba; Wikipedia (Baba Yaga — Related figures)
research_notes: Attested in Polish folklore as Baba Jaga. The record copies the Russian appearance text verbatim; Polish variant has regional flavor (Masovia, oak groves) but core attributes are shared.

description: The Chureca is a Virgin Islands death-omen spirit appearing as an owl-like creature. Its cry or appearance near a home predicts imminent death in the household. A localized variant of the widespread Caribbean 'owl as death messenger' belief (cf. Jamaican rolling calf, Haitian loogaroo owl form). Not to be confused with La Chureca, the Managua landfill.
source: Virgin Islands oral tradition; Caribbean folklore compilations (Parsons, Folk-Tales of Andros Island); comparative Caribbean owl-omen beliefs
research_notes: Attested in Virgin Islands folklore as an owl death omen. The name 'Chureca' may be a local creole term. The record's 'beast' type and 'forest-spirit' archetype are acceptable for an omen bird.

description: The Rolling Cauldron is a Jamaican magical object — a cauldron that rolls along roads and crossroads at night. It contains either treasure or a curse depending on whether one touches it. A road-spirit motif warning against greed and nocturnal travel. Part of Jamaican 'duppy' (ghost) folklore complex.
source: Jamaican folklore collections; Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories; comparative Caribbean rolling-object motifs; NALIS Trinidad Folklore Characters
research_notes: Attested in Jamaican oral tradition. The record's 'monster' type and 'forest-spirit' archetype are mismatches — it is a magical object/road spirit, not a creature.

description: Ti Malice (Little Malice) is the Haitian trickster, a clever hare who repeatedly outwits his greedy, slow-witted uncle Bouki (hyena). Originates from Senegalese Wolof/Fulani tales (Leuk the hare, Bouki the hyena) brought via the slave trade. Manipulates Bouki's greed to steal food, wives, and status. Louisiana equivalent: Lapin and Bouki. Embodies slave resistance through wit.
source: Teaching for Change, Haiti Literature; Gaudet, Bouki the Hyena in Louisiana and African Tales (JAF 1992); Stephen-Alexis retellings; Wikipedia (Ti Malice and Bouki)
research_notes: Well-attested in Haitian Creole oral tradition. The record's 'shapeshifter' archetype is incorrect — Ti Malice is a human/hare trickster figure, not a shapeshifter. 'Infiltration, wind control' strengths are fabrications.

description: Not independently attested in Jamaican tradition. The record's description ('Important cultural figure in Kiowa tradition') refers to the Kiowa (Native American Plains people), not Jamaica. Jamaica's trickster is Anansi (Kwaku Anansi), the West African spider trickster brought via the slave trade. This entry appears to be a fabricated or garbled conflation.
source: Kiowa oral tradition (Native American); Jamaican folklore (Anansi); no Jamaican source for a generic 'Trickster' entity
research_notes: The creature as described does not exist in Jamaican folklore. 'Trickster' is a role, not a named entity. Kiowa Trickster (Saynday) is a distinct Native American figure. Closest real analogue: Anansi (Jamaica) or Saynday (Kiowa). Recommend removal or merge with anansi-jamaica.

description: Anansi (Kwaku Anansi) is the Jamaican trickster spider, brought from Akan/Ashanti Ghana via the slave trade. Acquired all stories from sky god Nyame by capturing python, hornets, leopard, and fairy Mmoatia. Shape-shifts between spider and human; wife Aso, sons Ntikuma et al. Symbol of slave resistance and cultural survival. Tales end with proverbs ('If yuh cyaan ketch Kwaku, yuh ketch him shut').
source: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales; Haley, A Story a Story (Caldecott); Marshall, Anansi's Journey; Levine, Black Culture and Consciousness; Wikipedia (Anansi); NALIS Trinidad Folklore
research_notes: Best-documented Caribbean trickster. The record is accurate. 'Infiltration, wind control' strengths are modern gaming additions; folklore emphasizes cunning, storytelling, and wit.

description: The Mahogany Tree in Antiguan folklore is a sacred tree believed to be the dwelling of protective ancestral spirits. A powerful chief sacrificed himself, transforming into the tree to guard his people. Symbolizes strength, endurance, and protection. Reflects West African tree-spirit beliefs (e.g., Iroko, Silk Cotton) transplanted to the Caribbean.
source: Antiguan oral tradition; comparative Caribbean tree-spirit beliefs (Silk Cotton, Ceiba); West African sacred tree traditions (Iroko, Odan)
research_notes: Attested in Antiguan folklore as a sacred ancestral tree. The record's 'deity' type and 'shapeshifter' archetype are category errors — it is a sacred tree/ancestor vessel, not a shapeshifting deity.

description: Mama Dlo (Mother of Waters) is the Saint Lucian water spirit, upper body a beautiful woman with long flowing hair perpetually combing, lower body serpentine. Inhabits mountain pools and streams. A Caribbean manifestation of the West African Mami Wata/Mama Wata tradition brought by enslaved Africans. Can grant wealth or drown the disrespectful. Connects to Haitian Simbi and Guyanese Watra-mama.
source: Saint Lucian folklore; Drewal, Mami Wata: Arts for Water Spirits; Van Stipriaan, Watramama/Mami Wata; Anatol, The Things That Fly in the Night; Wikipedia (Mami Wata, Mama Dlo)
research_notes: Well-attested as Saint Lucian Mami Wata variant. The record's 'mountain' habitat tag is accurate (mountain pools). 'Drowning, luring' behaviors fit the ambivalent water spirit archetype.

description: The Mermaids of Black Rocks are vengeful mermaids said to inhabit the volcanic Black Rocks on the northeastern coast of Saint Kitts. They lure sailors with enchanting songs to drag them to watery graves. A localized Caribbean mermaid belief warning of sea dangers; the rock formation itself is a real landmark. May protect the island in some tellings.
source: Saint Kitts oral tradition; NALIS Trinidad Folklore Characters; Caribbean mermaid lore compilations; comparative Lesser Antilles coastal legends
research_notes: Attested in Kittitian folklore as a place-specific mermaid legend. The record is accurate. 'Vengeful' and 'enchant' behaviors are well-supported.

description: Le Zandolite is a Haitian spectral dragonfly appearing at night. If caught, it grants one wish before disappearing. A wish-granting animal spirit motif in Haitian folklore. Name may derive from French 'zandoli' (lizard/gecko) + diminutive, or creole variation. Not a major figure; minor wish-granting spirit.
source: Haitian folklore collections; comparative Caribbean wish-granting spirits (firefly, dragonfly); NALIS Trinidad Folklore Characters
research_notes: Attested as a minor Haitian spirit. The record's 'animal-spirit' type and 'forest-spirit' archetype are acceptable. 'Strength, stamina' strengths are generic filler not specific to this entity.

description: Loogaroo (Lougarou, Ligaroo, Lagahoo) is a Caribbean skin-shedding vampire derived from French 'loup-garou' (werewolf). By day a reclusive woman; by night she sheds her skin (hidden under a silk cotton tree), becomes a fireball, and flies to suck blood to fulfill a pact with the Devil (Bazil). Salt in the mortar destroys her.
source: Métraux, Voodoo in Haiti; Derby, Imperial Idols; Jenkins, Paradox of Blackness; Bunson, Vampire Encyclopedia; NALIS Trinidad Folklore Characters; Cleary, Mauritius; Wikipedia (Loogaroo, Soucouyant)
research_notes: Well-documented across Lesser Antilles. The record's 'shapeshifter' type fits; 'Dominica' culture is one locus (also Trinidad, Haiti, Guadeloupe). 'Deception, soul sight' strengths are generic vampire traits.

description: Lougawou is the Haitian Vodou werewolf/shapeshifter. By night, a practitioner (usually female) sends out her soul or transforms into animals (dog, cat, bird) to attack enemies or drain blood. Distinct from the fireball Loogaroo; lougawou emphasizes animal transformation via Vodou ritual. Related to Dominican Galipote (shapeshifter of animals and objects). Feared as a nocturnal predator.
source: Métraux, Voodoo in Haiti; Hurston, Tell My Horse; Derby, Imperial Idols; Haitian Vodou ethnography; Wikipedia (Loogaroo — Haiti section)
research_notes: Attested in Haitian Vodou practice. The record's 'werewolf' type is a loose gloss; 'shapeshifter' is more accurate. Distinct from loogaroo (fireball vampire) though related etymologically.

description: Lusca is the Bahamian sea monster of Andros Island's blue holes. Described as a gigantic octopus, cuttlefish, or half-shark half-octopus hybrid over 75 feet long. Name clipped from Mollusca. Drags swimmers and boats into blue holes. Investigated by Jeremy Wade (River Monsters) as likely a large octopus. Cautionary tale for blue hole divers. Inspired Lusca Fantastic Film Fest (Puerto Rico).
source: A Book of Creatures (lusca entry); Wade, River Monsters 'Terror in Paradise'; Bahamian oral tradition; Wikipedia (Lusca); Stranded Deep/City of Heroes game references
research_notes: Attested in Bahamian folklore as a blue hole monster. The record's 'monster' type and 'water-spirit' archetype are acceptable. 'Grounding, raw power' strengths are gaming filler.
